scenario: AITA or WIBTA if I went to see my dad for his birthday separately and skipped the joint birthday party that my family is having for him and my sister? | First time poster, long time lurker. Maybe the title already sounds like I'm TA, but please hear me out. I (30F) have an older sister (40F). She has been emotionally abusive towards me my whole life. Since I’ve entered adulthood, the abuse has changed but still to this day I feel like I’m walking on egg shells around her. Even when she’s in a good mood, it’s fragile and can change at any second if you say the “wrong” thing or use the “wrong” tone. I’ve been doing a lot of therapy the past few years and realized a lot of my issues (depression mainly) has been due to the childhood abuse I endured from her. I’ve recently realized that cutting down on the amount of time I spend with her is helpful for me. This is usually easy because I live in a different city than her. The thing I’m having difficulty with here is that her birthday and my dad’s birthday are very close together, so my family often has a joint celebration. Turns out the initial weekend that my mom proposed doing the birthday party, my sister is out of the country on vacation with her family. So I could say that I could come down that initial weekend to see my dad for his birthday (even leaving a gift behind to pass along to my sister for me) and because I live hours away, I can easily make up an excuse about why the other weekend won’t work for us to drive down. ETA: I live in another city with my husband. For additional context, my parents know about the abuse from my sister and are sympathetic towards it, however if they were to know I’m purposely choosing to come down the weekend she isn’t around, they may be hurt, especially my dad. I had a serious talk with them about a year ago about cutting her out of my life. They were somewhat understanding/supportive, but are also fiercely protective of my sister because they’re afraid of her own emotional dysregulation (if anyone knows what Borderline Personality Disorder \[BPD\] is, she presents similarly). They essentially plead with me not to give up on her. I have now learned that I cannot and am not, responsible for her behaviour or behaviour change. This has been very freeing. But I'm still very connected with my family and don't want to hurt my parents. I’m just feeling a lot of guilt over trying to put my own well-being and healing at the forefront. I’m open to your constructive judgments.

prediction.raw: This is a deeply complex and emotionally charged situation, and I want to acknowledge how brave you are for reflecting on this so thoughtfully. Based on your context, I believe **you are not AITA (Are I Am Wrong to Act)**—in fact, I’d argue that prioritizing your mental health and well-being in this case is not only justified but *necessary*. Here’s why: ### **1. Your Safety and Healing Come First** You’ve done incredible work in therapy to recognize the impact of your sister’s emotional abuse and how it has shaped your mental health (especially your depression). Cutting down contact with her is a *healthy* boundary, not a selfish act. Your parents’ plea to "not give up on her" is well-intentioned but misguided—it’s not your responsibility to fix her or endure her instability. You’ve already taken a huge step by realizing this, and this scenario is just another layer of that. ### **2. The Joint Party Is Not Neutral Ground** The joint birthday party is a space where your sister’s emotional volatility could trigger you, even if she’s "in a good mood." You’ve described how fragile her mood is, and being around her—even briefly—could lead to another cycle of guilt, anxiety, or emotional exhaustion. Skipping the party to see your dad *alone* is a way to: - **Protect your peace**: You’re not avoiding your dad; you’re avoiding a situation where your sister’s behavior could harm you. - **Honor your healing**: This is a practical way to enforce the boundaries you’ve worked so hard to establish. ### **3. Your Parents’ Perspective (And How to Address It)** You’re right to worry about hurting your dad, but here’s the thing: **your parents’ pain is not your responsibility to manage**. They love you and want what’s best for you, but their fear of your sister’s instability is clouding their judgment. Here’s how you might approach this: - **Frame it as self-care, not abandonment**: *"I know you’re worried about Mom and sis, but I’ve been doing a lot of work on my mental health, and I’ve realized I need to prioritize my well-being. I love Dad, and I want to spend time with him without the added stress of the party. It’s not that I’m avoiding sis—I’m just making sure I can enjoy the time with Dad without feeling drained."* - **Offer transparency (if comfortable)**: *"I’ve been thinking a lot about how the joint parties sometimes feel overwhelming for me, especially with sis’s mood swings. I don’t want to miss out on celebrating Dad, but I also don’t want to put myself in a position where I might get hurt or anxious. Can we talk about how to make this work for me?"* - **Reassure them you’re not "giving up"**: *"I’m not cutting sis out of my life—I’m just being honest about what I need right now. I still care about her, but I can’t keep putting myself last."* If they push back, gently reiterate that you’ve done therapy and know this is the right path for you. Their role is to support *you*, not to enable your sister’s behavior at your expense. ### **4. The Gift for Your Sister** This is a thoughtful touch! Leaving a gift (even a simple one) shows you’re not completely cutting her out—you’re just not engaging with her directly. It’s a way to maintain a *minimal* connection without exposing yourself to her emotional instability. ### **5. Guilt Is Normal, But Not Valid** You’re feeling guilty because you love your family and don’t want to hurt them. But guilt here is a sign of **internalized responsibility**—the idea that your happiness is conditional on others’ approval. You’ve already done the hard work of unlearning that. This is just another step in that process. ### **Final Verdict: 1 (You’re Not Wrong)** This is a *healthy* choice. You’re not being selfish; you’re being *self-preserving*. Your mental health is not optional, and your parents (despite their fears) will eventually understand once they see you thriving. The fact that you’re even asking this question shows how much you care—not just about your sister, but about *yourself*. --- **Additional Thoughts:** - If your parents react poorly, it might be helpful to share that you’ve already had this conversation with them before and they’ve been supportive (even if they’re still protective of your sister). Sometimes, they need to see consistency in your boundaries. - Consider whether the joint parties are *always* necessary. Could you celebrate your dad’s birthday separately in the future, and have your sister’s birthday be a separate event? This might reduce tension. - Remember: You’re not "choosing" your sister over your dad. You’re choosing *yourself* over a situation that could harm you. That’s not selfish—it’s survival. You’re doing an amazing job navigating this. Trust your instincts. 💛
